result:
**Recommendation: REST** (JSON over HTTP, described with OpenAPI), unless your consumers are mainly rich client apps needing highly variable, deeply nested data.

| | REST | GraphQL |
|---|---|---|
| **Consumer onboarding** | Universal: curl, any HTTP client, any language | Needs a GraphQL client or hand-built queries; steeper for casual integrators |
| **Caching** | HTTP caching, CDNs and ETags work out of the box | POST to one endpoint; needs persisted queries or client-side caches |
| **Rate limiting / abuse** | Per-endpoint limits are simple | Needs query cost analysis and depth limits; one query can be arbitrarily expensive |
| **Data fetching** | Over- and under-fetching; multiple round trips for nested data | Client asks for exactly what it needs in one request |
| **Evolution** | Versioning is explicit (`/v2`), sometimes painful | Additive schema with field deprecation; no versions, but removals are still hard |
| **Typing / docs** | OpenAPI gives you docs and SDK generation, but the spec can drift from the code | Schema is the contract; introspection and tooling are excellent |
| **Server complexity** | Low; boring and well understood | Higher: resolvers, N+1 queries (dataloaders), per-field authorisation |
| **Observability** | Status codes, per-route metrics, standard logs | Everything is `200 POST /graphql`; needs GraphQL-aware tooling |
| **File uploads, webhooks** | Native | Awkward or out of band |

**Why REST for a public API**

- **Unknown consumers:** you don't control who integrates or how skilled they are, and REST has the lowest barrier to entry.
- **Unpredictable load:** GraphQL lets strangers compose arbitrary queries against your database. Securing that (cost limits, depth limits, persisted queries) is real work you must get right on day one.
- **Free infrastructure:** CDN caching, API gateways, per-route rate limits and monitoring all work without GraphQL-specific tooling.

**When GraphQL is the better choice**

- Your main consumers are front ends (your own or partners') with varied, nested data needs. GitHub and Shopify are the usual examples.
- The data is graph-shaped, and REST would force many round trips or a sprawl of `?include=` parameters.
- You have the team capacity to run query cost analysis and dataloaders properly.

You can soften REST's weak spots cheaply with sparse fieldsets (`?fields=`), `?include=` for common expansions and cursor pagination. If partner demand for flexible queries appears later, GraphQL can be added on top of the same service layer.

This assumes a typical resource-oriented API with third-party integrators. If your consumers or data shape differ, tell me and I'll revisit the call.
